query: RAFT vs retrieval-only persona simulation can you match person without weight updates
answer: RAFT (Retrieval‑Augmented Fine‑Tuning) improves persona simulation by fine‑tuning the model’s parameters on examples that pair queries with both relevant and irrelevant retrieved documents, teaching the model how to weight, filter, and reason over that external context; this weight update yields more stable and consistent persona behavior even as conversations grow longer. A pure retrieval‑only approach—where the base model is left unchanged and a persona is supplied only through retrieved passages or prompts—can match a person to some extent but relies entirely on the quality of the retrieved text and the model’s innate ability to follow prompts, which often leads to drift, inconsistency, and hallucinations when the retriever brings in noisy or unrelated information. Consequently, without any weight updates you cannot achieve the same level of reliable, persona‑consistent responses that RAFT provides, though retrieval‑only can be useful for quick prototyping when weight‑change is prohibited.

results.title: RAFT: Retrieval-Augmented Fine-Tuning for AI Engineers | Aishwarya Srinivasan posted on the topic | LinkedIn
results.content:
D2L opens a middle path. It uses a hypernetwork to embed knowledge - purchase history, product context, consumer profiles - directly into the model's weights, in under a second. No retrieval pipeline. No bloated context window.
That means:
- The context window stays free for actual conversation
- Persona consistency doesn't degrade with conversation length
- You get close to the simplicity of prompt-based methods with much of the robustness of data-grounded ones
For prototyping and experimentation, this is a meaningful shift.
But there's an important caveat. [...] If you’re an AI engineer working on RAG, or building advanced retrieval-augmented systems, you need to know about RAFT: Retrieval-Augmented Fine-Tuning.
Let’s break it down 👇
→ Closed-Book Models (SFT Only)
The model learns everything at train time, and answers based purely on its internal weights. Fast, but brittle – hallucinations spike when the model faces unfamiliar queries.
→ Open-Book Models (Standard RAG)
At inference time, the model retrieves top-k documents and answers using them as context. But the model has never seen these docs during training – so it treats relevant and irrelevant documents the same way, often leading to noisy outputs.
→ RAFT: Retrieval + Fine-Tuning Combined [...] If you’re an AI engineer working on RAG, or building advanced retrieval-augmented systems, you need to know about RAFT: Retrieval-Augmented Fine-Tuning.
Let’s break it down 👇
→ Closed-Book Models (SFT Only)
The model learns everything at train time, and answers based purely on its internal weights. Fast, but brittle – hallucinations spike when the model faces unfamiliar queries.
→ Open-Book Models (Standard RAG)

RAFT focuses on a narrower but increasingly popular domain than the general open book exam, called the domain-specific open-book exam. In domain-specific open book exam, we know a priori the domain in which the LLM will be tested --- used for inference. The LLM can respond to the users' prompt using use any and all information from this specific domain, which it has been fine-tuned on.
Examples of domain specific examples include enterprise documents, latest news, code repositories belonging to an organization, etc.
In all these scenarios, the LLM will be used to respond to the questions, whose answers can be found within a collection of documents (a small practical domain). The retrieval technique itself has little to no-impact on the mechanism (though it may impact the accuracy). 1.   Data Construction

 Each training sample contains:

   A query (e.g., _“How much parental leave does IBM offer?”_)
   A set of documents (both relevant and irrelevant)
   A gold answer
   _Core documents_ contain relevant context (e.g., HR policies on leave).
   _Tangent documents_ contain irrelevant information (e.g., retirement plans).

By mixing these together, RAFT simulates real-world RAG scenarios where retrieval isn’t perfect.

2. Document Sets

 Two types of sets are created:

   Set 1 → Core + tangent documents (realistic retrieval noise).

results.title: RAFT: Sailing Llama towards better domain-specific RAG
results.content:
Both approaches have limitations. With fine-tuning, the model is not only limited to what it has been trained on, but it is also subject to approximation and hallucination. With RAG, the model is grounded, that is, its responses are based on some reference documents in a corpus. These reference documents are retrieved based on their semantic similarity to the query; the model doesn’t actually know which documents are truly relevant or are just red herrings. These “distractor” documents may be pulled into the model’s context even when they are not good sources for a well-reasoned answer. [...] In this article, we will look at the limitations of those two approaches and how a team of UC Berkeley researchers, Tianjun Zhang and Shishir G. Patil, may have just discovered a better approach. The Berkeley team also published a blog post about the paper explaining the advantages and disadvantages of the previous approaches and how the RAFT approach produces more effective results. The RAFT paper implementation is available in their GitHub repository.
